KTS is the prototype of complex overgrowth disorder associated with vascular anomalies and is the most common of these disorders. While there is phenotypic overlay, KTS has specific clinical and radiologic findings that separate it from other complex combination vascular anomalies syndromes such as Congenital Lipomatous Overgrowth, Vascular Malformations, Epidermal Nevis, Spinal/Skeletal Anomalies/Scoliosis syndrome (CLOVES), Proteus, Capillary Venous Malformation (CVM) with overgrowth, Diffuse Capillary Malformation with overgrowth (DCMO), and Parkes Weber syndrome. KTS manifests as a cluster of congenital malformations affecting the limb(s) and pelvis. It typically affects the lower extremity unilaterally. Nevertheless, KTS may occasionally affect the upper extremity or both legs. Upper extremity presentation has previously been referred to as thoracic or truncal KTS; many of those patients are now diagnosed as CLOVES. Involvement of the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts is also common in KTS. Institutional knowledge and experience of our interdisciplinary Vascular Anomalies Center (VAC) at Boston Children's Hospital was consolidated through managing and studying a large cohort of patients with KTS. Nevertheless, the strength of evidence based on the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine for the major categories (diagnosis, prognosis and therapy/prevention) in general are either level 4 or 5, which refers respectively to "case-series" and "expert opinion" without explicit critical appraisal. Despite the presence of more than 1,000 published articles, lack of clear diagnostic criteria, misdiagnoses and misconceptions are still common in the published literature about KTS. Authors Affiliations * 1 University of Central Florida College of Medicine, 6850 Lake Nona Blvd, Orlando, FL, USA 32827. Electronic address: Nimaipatel99@gmail.com. * 2 Arnold Palmer Hospital for Children, 1725 Cook Ave, Orlando 32806, FL, USA. * 3 Nemours Children's Hospital, 3535 Nemours Pkwy, Orlando 32827, FL, USA. * PMID: 32559682 * DOI: 10.1016/j.clinimag.2020.06.011 Abstract Background: Klippel-Trenaunay Syndrome (KTS) is a genetic vascular malformation disorder which induces a variety of phenotypic expression in patients which differ in terms of severity/location. While previous studies have documented genitourinary (GU) complications in adult KTS patients, documentation of the scope and incidence of GU involvement in the pediatric population with imaging findings is currently limited. This study represents the largest KTS genitourinary review to date. Objective: To assess the incidence, scope, clinical findings and imaging characteristics of GU pathology in pediatric KTS patients. Materials/methods: Using a retrospective data analysis design, the charts and imaging studies of pediatric KTS patients were reviewed. All patients received care at a specialized vascular clinic within a multicenter tertiary care system. Variables studied included age, age at KTS diagnosis, gender, urologic involvement, and age of urologic complication. Results: 58 patients were identified. 33 were male and 25 were female. 10 patients had GU findings. Three of these patients had multifocal GU involvement (greater than 1 finding). Urologic manifestations were diverse with 9 distinct diagnoses involving 6 unique organs. Renal, vesical and scrotal pathologies were most common. Hematuria was the most common presenting symptom in 30% (3/10). Previously unreported findings (labial swelling, renal lymphatic cysts) were identified. The average age of KTS diagnosis was 4.9 years. The average age of documented GU complication and involvement was 7.6 years. Conclusion: Significant GU complications due to KTS can occur in the pediatric population. Early clinical and imaging characterization of these conditions is important for management, family education and early intervention strategies. Genitourinary Surgery and Interventions Volume 12 - 2025 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fsurg.2025.1532509 Genitourinary involvement in Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome: pathophysiology, evaluation, and management * WL Weilong Lin * CX Chong Xie * HW Huaijie Wang * * WY Weijia Yang * PW Peihua Wang * ZG Zhengtuan Guo * Department of Pediatric Surgery and Vascular Anomalies, Xi’an International Medical Center Hospital, Xi’an, China Article metrics View details Abstract Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome (KTS) typically involves a combination of capillary, lymphatic, and venous malformations of the lower extremities. Genitourinary involvement is frequently observed in patients with KTS. Bleeding and pelvic pain are the most common complications. This condition has been increasingly reported in recent years. However, most authors have only depicted extreme presentations or various combinations of clinical findings. The underlying pathophysiology of genitourinary involvement in KTS remains unclear. Genitourinary involvement in female patients with KTS has a more complicated pathophysiology than that in male patients with KTS. After understanding its pathophysiology, some patients can be successfully managed by using a staged plan. Therefore, recognizing the pathophysiology of genitourinary involvement is necessary for practitioners to evaluate and determine adequate management. Owing to the complexity and rarity of this condition, a prospective controlled study involving a large cohort of patients is impossible. Based on a literature review and our practice, we discuss the pathophysiology, evaluation, and treatment strategies for genitourinary involvement in KTS. Introduction Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome (KTS) is a rare congenital disorder, characterized by combination of capillary-lymphatic-venous malformations (1). It typically affects the lower extremities unilaterally and occasionally involves the upper or bilateral lower extremities. It can also affect the pelvic organs, abdomen, or trunk (1–3). Gastrointestinal and genitourinary (GU) involvement is common, with an incidence of more than 30% in patients (1, 2, 4). Gastrointestinal and GU involvement can be asymptomatic and can manifest as recurrent hemorrhage of the affected organs, ranging from occult to massive and life-threatening blood loss (1, 2, 4–6). GU involvement usually manifests as hematuria, dysmenorrhea, and menorrhagia (2, 4). Women with KTS and uterine involvement are at significant risk of severe postpartum hemorrhage (7, 8). However, these presentations remain challenging and require multidisciplinary management. Under these conditions, venous malformations (VM) infiltrate and surround the walls of the GU system, causing pain and hemorrhage. The management of hematuria and menorrhagia is conservative but dysmenorrhea in KTS patients can be treated pharmacologically (4). However, if problematic hemorrhage and dysmenorrhea develop, invasive treatments for the bleeding sites or affected organs are preferred, including surgical resection of the involved organ (4, 9–11), interventional embolization (12, 13), and sclerotherapy (14, 15). Many patients with KTS with GU involvement have been reported in the literature; however, most authors have only depicted extreme manifestations or illustrated various interesting combinations of signs, symptoms, laboratory tests, images, and complications of KTS (5, 6, 16–52). Owing to the complexity, rarity, and under-recognized pathophysiology of GU involvement in KTS, an integrated management strategy for various treatments has not been established. No recommendations exist for the management of GU involvement in patients with KTS. GU involvement in female patients has a more complicated pathophysiology than that of male patients with KTS (Figure 1). KTS can also affect the left ovary and its venous system. Of note, malformation and reflux of the uterine veins can also cause noncyclic pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea (53). Practitioners must be aware of the underlying pathophysiology of GU involvement in patients with KTS to improve their management. These vein malformations and reflux have been under-recognized in patients with KTS with pelvic involvement (2). Factors contributing to this lack of recognition include the rarity and complexity of pelvic VM in KTS, the challenge of distinguishing pelvic involvement in KTS from common pelvic venous disorders in adult women, the absence of validated diagnostic modalities and condition-specific treatment approaches, and limited reports on effective treatments. MRI can easily differentiate the anatomical differences of pelvic veins from veins in KTS (1). In a recent paper (1), we comprehensively discussed and reviewed the pathophysiology, evaluation, and management of gastrointestinal involvement in KTS. In this paper, we review and discuss its pathophysiology and propose an evaluation and treatment strategy that can help manage KTS with GU involvement. Mini-report on the main genitourinary complications of KTS

The genitourinary complications of Klippel–Trenaunay Syndrome (KTS) are best understood as a combination of vascular and lymphatic changes affecting the urinary tract, genital tract, and pelvic structures. The available evidence consistently highlights that genitourinary involvement is “frequently observed” in KTS and is often associated with bleeding, pelvic pain, and a broad spectrum of anatomical and functional abnormalities [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R4][N4-F3].

Specific urinary tract complications include hematuria and GU bleeding from vascular anomalies. One cohort study noted hematuria as the most common presenting symptom in 30% of pediatric KTS patients, and another review found that GU complications can manifest as recurrent hemorrhage from affected organs, ranging from occult to massive and life-threatening blood loss [N5-F1][N5-F2]. The urinary system can be involved in multiple ways: the study explicitly reports bladder involvement, urethral involvement, and kidney involvement in the same cohort, with hematuria arising from the bladder, urethra, and kidney [N5-F4]. However, the evidence base for hydronephrosis and ureteral abnormalities is thinner in the provided material; those specific terms are not directly supported in the excerpted sources, so any claim about them should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive.

Genital complications are more clearly documented. The evidence notes genital abnormalities, including cutaneous genital abnormalities and visceral genitourinary involvement [N5-F4]. The pediatric study also identifies “previously unreported findings” such as labial swelling and renal lymphatic cysts, suggesting that the genital tract is not limited to obvious malformations [N5-F1]. The Frontiers review explicitly lists genital and pelvic complications, and notes that female patients may have more complicated pathophysiology [N5-F2]. While the provided excerpts do not give a direct tally of phimosis, redundant foreskin, or vulvar malformations, they do support the broader conclusion that genital involvement can include both cutaneous and structural abnormalities, and that this is a recognized feature of KTS [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F3].

Vascular and lymphatic changes contribute to genitourinary dysfunction in several ways. First, vascular malformations can directly affect the urinary tract, bladder, penis, scrotum, vagina, and vulva, and may manifest as bleeding or other complications [N2-R1]. Second, lymphatic malformations can contribute to pelvic and genitourinary complications, with the guidelines emphasizing that KTS is a combination of capillary, lymphatic, and venous malformations [N2-R2][N2-R4]. Third, the Frontiers review explains that venous malformations can infiltrate and surround the walls of the GU system, causing pain and hemorrhage, and that pelvic venous malformations can cause noncyclic pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea [N5-F2]. The pediatric cohort study also notes diverse pathology in several locations due to lymphatic/venous malformation, reinforcing the idea that the genitourinary tract is a common target for these anomalies [N6-R4][N6-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a model in which KTS genitourinary complications arise from a mix of vascular and lymphatic disease affecting the urinary tract, genital tract, and pelvic structures, with bleeding and pelvic pain as the most commonly reported complications [N1-R1][N2-R1][N5-F2].

Mini-report on which patients are predominantly affected by KTS genitourinary complications

The available evidence suggests that genitourinary complications in KTS occur across a broad age range, but are especially prominent in pediatric patients. The largest pediatric cohort in the provided material included 58 KTS patients, with 10 having GU findings, and the average age of documented GU complication and involvement was 7.6 years [N5-F1]. Another pediatric study similarly emphasizes that significant GU complications can occur in the pediatric population and that early clinical and imaging characterization is important [N5-F1]. These findings suggest that GU complications are not confined to adulthood and may emerge in childhood, often after the initial diagnosis of KTS [N5-F1].

Age-related patterns are not fully quantified in the excerpts, but the evidence implies that complications may appear later in life after the disease is recognized. The pediatric cohort reports that the average age of KTS diagnosis was 4.9 years, whereas the average age of documented GU complication was 7.6 years [N5-F1]. This indicates that GU complications may not be immediately apparent at diagnosis and can develop later, possibly as the vascular and lymphatic changes evolve or as patients age [N5-F1]. The cohort also notes that hematuria was the most common presenting symptom in 30% of the 10 patients with GU findings, which suggests that some complications can appear early enough to be a first presenting symptom, while others may emerge later [N5-F1].

Sex differences in prevalence and severity are also present, though the evidence is not fully balanced. The guidelines note that KTS has no established racial or sex predilection, but the Frontiers review states that genitourinary involvement in female patients has a more complicated pathophysiology than in male patients [N3-R2][N5-F2]. The same review also notes that women with KTS and uterine involvement are at significant risk of severe postpartum hemorrhage [N5-F2]. The cohort study reports that 33 of 51 patients with cutaneous genital abnormalities experienced intermittent bleeding, with conservative management successful in 64% and excision required in 36% [N5-F4]. The gender distribution in that cohort was 33 males and 25 females, but the excerpt does not provide a sex-specific breakdown of GU complication severity, so any conclusion about sex differences must be cautious [N5-F1].

Anatomically, the most commonly involved regions are the urinary tract, genital tract, and pelvic structures. The pediatric study reports renal, vesical, and scrotal pathologies as most common, and the Frontiers review notes hematuria, dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, and pelvic pain as major complications [N5-F1][N5-F2]. The cohort also reports bladder, urethra, and kidney involvement, with hematuria arising from these sites [N5-F4]. Genitally, the evidence supports cutaneous genital abnormalities, visceral GU involvement, and previously unreported findings such as labial swelling and renal lymphatic cysts [N5-F1][N5-F4]. In female patients, the review also emphasizes uterine involvement and pelvic venous malformations as important contributors to complex pathophysiology [N5-F2].

In summary, the evidence points to pediatric patients as the predominant group affected by KTS genitourinary complications, with complications often appearing after the initial diagnosis and more commonly involving the urinary tract, genital tract, and pelvic structures. Female patients appear to have a more complex disease course, particularly when pelvic or uterine involvement is present [N5-F1][N5-F2].

Mini-report on evidence quality and clinical relevance

The evidence quality for KTS genitourinary complications is mixed. The strongest supporting evidence is cohort-based. The pediatric cohort study is explicitly described as a retrospective data analysis of 58 pediatric KTS patients and is noted as the largest KTS genitourinary review to date [N5-F1]. It provides age, gender, and complication data, and reports hematuria as the most common presenting symptom in 30% of the 10 patients with GU findings [N5-F1]. Another cohort study from Mayo Clinic reports that 30% of 218 KTS patients had genitourinary involvement, including cutaneous genital abnormalities, visceral GU involvement, and bladder/urethral/kidney hematuria, with substantial rates of intervention for complications [N5-F4]. These cohort findings are therefore better supported than isolated case reports and provide more reliable estimates of incidence and management needs [N5-F1][N5-F4].

Case reports and smaller studies are also present in the evidence base, but they are less informative for incidence and severity. The guidelines note that KTS is a rare congenital disorder and that the literature is heterogeneous, with prior reviews using data from diverse specialty-specific articles, which may have led to erroneous conclusions [N4-F3]. The Frontiers review similarly emphasizes that most authors have only depicted extreme presentations or combinations of clinical findings, and that the underlying pathophysiology remains unclear [N5-F2]. This suggests that many of the reported complications are based on case series or rare presentations rather than large, standardized studies.

The frequency with which genitourinary complications are recognized or reported in KTS appears to be increasing. The pediatric cohort study notes that GU complications in pediatric KTS have been limited in the literature, but it was the largest review to date [N5-F1]. The Frontiers review also states that GU involvement in KTS has been increasingly reported in recent years, and that it is frequently observed in patients with KTS [N1-R1][N5-F2]. The Mayo Clinic cohort study reports 30% genitourinary involvement, which the authors argue is triple the previously reported incidence of 9% [N5-F4]. Taken together, these findings indicate that genitourinary complications are not rare in KTS, but have historically been underrecognized or underreported in the literature [N5-F1][N5-F4].

Clinically, the evidence has major implications for diagnosis, monitoring, and multidisciplinary care. The guidelines stress that patients should be referred to a specialized center with experience in managing complex overgrowth and vascular anomalies, and that interdisciplinary assessment is needed for diagnosis and complication management [N4-F3]. The pediatric cohort study argues that early clinical and imaging characterization is important for management, family education, and early intervention [N5-F1]. The Frontiers review further emphasizes that practitioners need to understand the pathophysiology of GU involvement to improve management, and that multidisciplinary management is required because of the complexity, rarity, and lack of validated diagnostic and treatment approaches [N5-F2]. The Mayo Clinic cohort also shows that many patients require interventional therapy for complications, with 52% of those with urological manifestations eventually needing interventional therapy [N5-F4].

In terms of evidence quality, the most defensible conclusions come from cohort studies such as the pediatric and Mayo Clinic cohorts [N5-F1][N5-F4], while case reports and prior reviews provide important clinical observations but are less reliable for prevalence or severity [N4-F3][N5-F2]. The clinical relevance is clear: KTS genitourinary complications are important, can be severe, and require early recognition, imaging, and multidisciplinary care [N5-F1][N5-F2][N5-F4].

Klippel–Trenaunay Syndrome (KTS) is associated with a range of genitourinary complications that arise from the syndrome’s core vascular and lymphatic abnormalities. The evidence in the branch reports is consistent in three main conclusions: first, that genitourinary involvement is common and can be severe; second, that it affects a broad age range but especially stands out in pediatric patients; and third, that the complications are best understood as a mix of urinary tract, genital tract, and pelvic disease, with bleeding and pelvic pain as major features [N1-R1][N2-R1][N5-F2][N5-F4].

## 1) Main genitourinary complications associated with KTS

### Urinary tract complications
The most clearly documented urinary tract complications are hematuria and GU bleeding. A pediatric cohort study found hematuria as the most common presenting symptom in 30% of 10 patients with genitourinary findings, and the same study reported bladder, urethral, and kidney involvement, with hematuria arising from these sites [N5-F1][N5-F4]. The Frontiers review also notes that GU complications can manifest as recurrent hemorrhage from affected organs, ranging from occult to massive and life-threatening blood loss [N5-F2]. While hydronephrosis and ureteral abnormalities are plausible in the broader clinical picture, the provided evidence does not directly support them as specifically established complications; therefore, claims about them should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive [N5-F1][N5-F2].

### Genital complications
Genital complications are well documented in the evidence. The pediatric cohort study reports cutaneous genital abnormalities and visceral genitourinary involvement, and notes “previously unreported findings” such as labial swelling and renal lymphatic cysts [N5-F1][N5-F4]. The Frontiers review explicitly lists genital and pelvic complications and notes that female patients may have a more complicated pathophysiology than male patients [N5-F2]. Although the provided excerpts do not provide direct counts of phimosis, redundant foreskin, or vulvar malformations, they do support the broader conclusion that genital involvement can include both cutaneous and structural abnormalities [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R4][N6-R5].

### Vascular and lymphatic contribution to dysfunction
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that KTS is a combination of capillary, lymphatic, and venous malformations, and that these anomalies can affect the urinary tract, bladder, penis, scrotum, vagina, and vulva [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The Frontiers review explains that venous malformations can infiltrate and surround the walls of the GU system, causing pain and hemorrhage, and that pelvic venous malformations can cause noncyclic pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea [N5-F2]. The pediatric cohort study similarly notes diverse pathology in several locations due to lymphatic/venous malformation [N6-R4][N6-R5]. In short, vascular and lymphatic changes are central to genitourinary dysfunction in KTS, often by directly damaging or compressing pelvic and urinary structures and by creating a proclivity for bleeding and pain [N2-R1][N5-F2].

## 2) Which patients are predominantly affected by KTS genitourinary complications?

### Age groups and timing of complications
The evidence suggests that genitourinary complications are not confined to adulthood and are especially prominent in pediatric patients. The largest pediatric cohort in the provided material included 58 KTS patients, with 10 having GU findings, and the average age of documented GU complication and involvement was 7.6 years [N5-F1]. Another pediatric study similarly emphasizes that significant GU complications can occur in the pediatric population and that early clinical and imaging characterization is important [N5-F1]. This indicates that GU complications may appear after the initial diagnosis of KTS, often later in childhood or adolescence, rather than always being immediately apparent at diagnosis [N5-F1]. The cohort also notes that hematuria was the most common presenting symptom in 30% of the 10 patients with GU findings, showing that some complications can present early enough to be a first clinical sign, while others may emerge later [N5-F1].

### Sex differences
Sex differences are present in the evidence, though they are not fully quantified. The guidelines note that KTS has no established racial or sex predilection [N3-R2]. However, the Frontiers review states that genitourinary involvement in female patients has a more complicated pathophysiology than in male patients [N5-F2]. It also notes that women with KTS and uterine involvement are at significant risk of severe postpartum hemorrhage [N5-F2]. The cohort study reports a gender distribution of 33 males and 25 females among patients with cutaneous genital abnormalities, but the excerpt does not provide a sex-specific breakdown of complication severity, so conclusions about severity differences should be cautious [N5-F1]. Overall, the evidence suggests that females may be more likely to present with complex or pelvic-specific complications, especially when uterine or pelvic venous involvement is present [N5-F2].

### Most commonly involved anatomical regions
The most commonly involved anatomical regions are the urinary tract, genital tract, and pelvic structures.
